text: India stands at a crossroads in its development journey. The choices we make today about technology, industrialisation, and resource allocation will determine the trajectory of our nation for the next half century. I am firmly convinced that we must not follow the slow, incremental path of industrialisation that the Western nations took over two centuries. We have the opportunity — indeed, the obligation — to leapfrog. By applying the most advanced technologies directly to our most pressing problems, we can compress decades of development into years. This is not a pipe dream; it is a practical strategy grounded in the realities of modern science.

The role of science in national development cannot be overstated, but neither should it be mystified. Science is not magic. It is a method — a disciplined, systematic approach to understanding the world and solving problems. When we apply scientific methods to agriculture, we get the Green Revolution. When we apply them to public health, we eradicate diseases. When we apply them to communication, we connect a billion people. The key is not just scientific knowledge, but scientific thinking — the ability to define problems precisely, gather data rigorously, test hypotheses honestly, and implement solutions systematically.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Address to the Indian Science Congress, 1967

text: Industrial development in India must be guided by a dual commitment: to modern technology and to social equity. The establishment of ATIRA — the Ahmedabad Textile Industry's Research Association — exemplifies this approach. The textile industry is India's largest employer, but it faces serious challenges of efficiency, quality, and competitiveness. Through ATIRA, we bring scientific research methods to bear on these challenges. We develop new processes, test new materials, train workers, and help traditional industries modernise without losing their essential character or their workforce.

The concept of self-reliance that we pursue is not autarky or isolation. We do not seek to cut ourselves off from the world. On the contrary, we seek to engage with the world from a position of strength and competence. Self-reliance means building the indigenous capability to understand, evaluate, adapt, and improve upon the best that the world has to offer. It means training our scientists and engineers to be creative contributors to global knowledge, not passive recipients. When India achieves self-reliance in space technology, we will not stop collaborating with other nations — we will collaborate as equals.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, National Self-Reliance Policy Speech, 1969

text: Nuclear energy represents one of the most powerful tools available to a developing nation. The energy needs of a country like India are enormous and growing rapidly. Our coal reserves, while substantial, are finite and geographically concentrated. Hydroelectric power is limited by geography and monsoon variability. Nuclear energy offers a path to abundant, clean, and reliable power that can drive industrialisation across the country. The work that Dr. Bhabha initiated at the Atomic Energy Commission has laid a strong foundation, and it is our responsibility to build upon it with the same vision and determination.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Atomic Energy Commission Address, 1966

text: The electronics industry in India is at a critical juncture. The world is entering an age where electronic systems will pervade every aspect of life — from communication and transportation to healthcare and education. India must not be left behind in this revolution. As Chairman of the Electronics Committee, I have recommended a comprehensive strategy that includes establishing semiconductor manufacturing, building a strong base in computer technology, and training a large cadre of electronic engineers and technicians. The investment required is modest compared to the returns, but the window of opportunity will not remain open indefinitely.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Electronics Committee Report to Government, 1967

text: International cooperation in science is not merely desirable — it is essential. The problems facing humanity are too vast and too complex for any single nation to address alone. Climate, disease, food security, energy — these are global challenges that demand global solutions. India's participation in international scientific programmes is not charity; it is enlightened self-interest. By contributing to global scientific knowledge, we gain access to a vastly larger pool of expertise and resources than we could ever create on our own.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, International Cooperation in Science Speech, 1969

text: A nation's true wealth is measured not by its GDP or its military power, but by the quality of its institutions and the capability of its people. Buildings can be built in months; institutions take decades to mature. The institutions that we are building today — PRL, ISRO, IIM, ATIRA, the Community Science Centre — are investments in India's future that will yield returns for generations. They will train leaders, produce innovations, solve problems, and inspire young people long after the individuals who founded them are forgotten.
